MTL 10: In this course, we will examine how international migration law functions as a technology of classification. To understand law's technological functions, we must (i) expand our notion of what technology "is," beyond the metallic/silicon and digital, and (ii) interrogate the categories of mobility migration law has naturalized in our everyday language, including distinctions between "economic migrants" and "genuine refugees." Course materials include a broad range of literature from legal studies, history of science, critical technology studies, and migration history; primary source documents such as legal instruments and judicial opinions; and works of creative nonfiction and film. While open to anyone interested in issues related to immigration and/or technology, this course is designed to be particularly useful for students considering law school in the future and law students/lawyers with blackletter law training who desire a more critical and humanistic orientation to the field. "Critical making" activities are a central part of this course, and the "engagement-based" grading system may be different from those you have experienced thus far in your educational career. Please read the syllabus - and the "Course Requirements" and "Grading Policy" sections in particular-carefully as you decide whether this course would be a good fit for you in light of your own learning goals and priorities.
MTL 11: Caste and gender are inseparable in how they animate South Asian society and culture from its ancient through postcolonial history. Thus, a combined understanding of caste and gender as co- constitutive logics and the long legacies of feminist, queer, and trans- Dalit-Bahujan resistance provide a crucial starting point for any anthropological, historical, political, economic, or cultural analyses of the region. How do caste and gender orchestrate each other? How do caste and gender relations change over time and across religious, ethnic, or national boundaries? How do they determine citizenship, legal personhood, and access to state infrastructure? How are experiences of caste, gender, and sexual identities communicated, consolidated, or complicated through popular media? In addressing such pivotal questions, this course surveys feminist, queer, and trans- approaches to Caste and Dalit Studies, exploring them through Indian cinema, both Bollywood and independently produced films. With weekly screenings as the basis for in-depth discussions, we will analyze each film alongside a selection of critical texts. The course will be particularly valuable for students whose work engages with the Indian subcontinent, South Asia, or its global diasporas, especially through comparative, transnational, or interdisciplinary approaches.
MTL 110: As Poet Laureate of San Mateo County and the author of Gentefication and the forthcoming collection The Right to Remain Violets (University of Arizona Press, 2026), Antonio Lopez invites students into a creative seminar on how poetry can speak back to power, history, and silence. This course explores poetry as both testimony and transformation - an art of survival that renders grief, memory, and resistance audible. Drawing inspiration from Lopez's own hybrid poetic practice, students will read across traditions of race and resistance, including Audre Lorde, June Jordan, Amiri Baraka, Gloria Anzaldua, Garrett Hongo, Claudia Rankine, Aracelis Girmay, and Ocean Vuong. Through weekly writing workshops, close readings, and community discussions, students will experiment with form and voice while considering how poetry functions as both witness and refuge. The course culminates in a final portfolio and reflective artist statement articulating each student's own rite to remain.
MTL 112: The videogame industry is worth hundreds of billions of dollars annually; the medium's prevalence and interactivity position it beyond entertainment. Born in research labs in the 1950s-60s, videogames have long served serious purposes, such as flight simulators used to train pilots. Moreover, their rule-based immersion can model complex systems, reveal trade-offs, and foster empathy through narrative, audio-visual design, and world-building. This War of Mine enters Poland's national curriculum to teach war from a civilian perspective, SPENT simulates daily choices under poverty, and Darfur is Dying highlights risks in refugee camps. So how can such games inform public understanding and help reimagine more equitable futures? This course turns game design into a laboratory for modeling, and even challenging, real-world inequalities. Students will design and prototype small, playable games that respond to community-based challenges, such as migration, war, housing, and health, translating design theories into practice through creative coding and storytelling. Projects are co-designed with community partners to support social change and civic engagement with practical, usable outcomes. By the end of the course, students will have completed the full game-design cycle: frame a real-world issue; map stakeholders and cause-effect loops between their actions; turn insights into rules and audiovisual narratives; playtest and iterate prototypes; and present publicly. Technically, students will learn Twine and/or Unity and publish a portfolio-ready build on itch.io. Along the way, they will strengthen entrepreneurial collaboration, problem-solving, and technical communication skills that translate to the Bay Area's civic-tech ecosystem. The course demonstrates how game design can produce concrete, usable tools that make a tangible difference.
MTL 334A: This is an interdisciplinary course introducing the primary contributions to the field of queer theory in the humanities. These readings will begin with Eve Sedgwick's work and responses to it from Heather Love, Jane Gallop, Jose Munoz, and Lauren Berlant. Then we will look at the work of Judith Butler and its impact on Performance Studies; readings here will include work by Phelan, Hart, and Halberstam. We will also consider queer theory's influence in Art History by reading texts by Norman Bryson, Jonathan Katz, Judith Bryan Wilson, and Richard Meyer (among others). We will also reflect on the critical discussion of why queer theory "failed." Readings will be by David Halperin and will also include President Trump's executive order mandating that the United States recognizes only two gender categories. In addition to reading and participating in all seminar meetings, students will be asked to give one short presentation of 20 minutes AND to serve as a respondent to the work of another student (10 minutes). These responses will serve to give students an opportunity to begin the difficult work of thinking across different fields. Final essays (15-20 pages) will engage with the material on the syllabus but they can be shaped in a way that best serves your overall interests and concerns.
MTL 334B: This course explores central topics in aesthetics where aesthetics is understood both in the narrow sense of the philosophy of art and aesthetic judgment, and in a broader sense as it relates to questions of perception, sensation, and various modes of embodied experience. We will engage with both classical and contemporary works in aesthetic theory, while special emphasis will be placed on phenomenological approaches to art and aesthetic experience across a range of media and/or mediums (including painting, sculpture, film, and digital media).
MTL 334C: Our course serves both as an introduction to graduate studies and as an introduction to interdisciplinary practice for entering PhD students in MTL at Stanford. Required for first-year graduate students, our course examines major historical and theoretical approaches to the interdisciplinary humanities via engagement with the living application of these approaches on campus. Additionally, we attend to contemporary debates about PhD study, higher education, and issues of professional development. At the end of the class you will have a clearer sense of the scholar you want to become and on concrete ways to develop your interests, navigate faculty mentor-grad relations, department cultures, and life-work balance. Non MTL graduate students will be accepted only with permission from the instructors.
